concepts.name: Article 6 Architecture: Three Pillars and Their Distinctions
key_dimensions: Distinction between Article 6.2 (bilateral/cooperative approaches), 6.4 (UN-supervised multilateral mechanism), and 6.8 (non-market approaches) — a classic UPSC trap on which is 'market' vs 'non-market'
Why Article 6.8 is explicitly non-market and what it covers (capacity building, technology transfer, climate finance)
Overlap and boundary confusion: when does a 6.2 bilateral deal shade into what 6.4 was meant to handle
COP26 Glasgow and COP27 Sharm el-Sheikh milestones in finalising Article 6 rulebook after years of deadlock

concepts.name: Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs) under Article 6.2
key_dimensions: Definition: ITMOs as the unit of transfer in cooperative approaches — not a carbon credit per se but an outcome-based unit
Who issues ITMOs: the host country (not the UN), making it a sovereign bilateral instrument — contrast with 6.4 credits issued by a UN body
Corresponding Adjustments (CA): mandatory for ITMOs to avoid double counting — the single most testable technical concept
Eligible uses of ITMOs: NDC achievement AND 'other international mitigation purposes' (OMIP) such as CORSIA — distinction matters for UPSC

concepts.name: Corresponding Adjustments (CA): Mechanism to Prevent Double Counting
key_dimensions: Core logic: selling country must add back the mitigation unit to its emissions (debit), buying country can subtract it — net global effect is zero shift
Why CA is mandatory under 6.2 and 6.4 but NOT required under 6.8 (non-market) — a classic 'only/except' trap
Difference between 'first transfer' CA trigger vs. 'authorization' trigger — nuance debated in Paris Agreement negotiations
Implications for host countries like India: selling ITMOs reduces headroom to meet own NDC targets — a sovereignty and strategic concern

concepts.name: Article 6.4 Mechanism: The New Centralised Carbon Market
key_dimensions: Governed by the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body under CMA (Conference of Parties serving as Meeting of Parties to Paris Agreement) — not under UNFCCC Secretariat directly
Two types of credits: A6.4ERs used for NDCs (with CA) vs. mitigation contribution units (MCUs) used for host country's own NDC — distinction is a UPSC trap
Transition of CDM projects to Article 6.4: eligibility criteria, cut-off dates, and which CDM credits (CERs) were grandfathered — India had large CDM portfolio
Role of Designated Operational Entities (DOEs) under 6.4 vs. CDM validators — continuity and change in institutional architecture

concepts.name: Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) vs. Article 6.4: Continuity and Rupture
key_dimensions: CDM was under Kyoto Protocol (developed vs. developing country binary); Article 6.4 is under Paris Agreement (all countries participate) — fundamental structural shift
CDM Certified Emission Reductions (CERs) vs. Article 6.4 Emission Reductions (A6.4ERs) — unit name change signals governance change
Additionality and baseline methodologies: Article 6.4 introduces 'standardised baselines' and 'conservative baselines' as improvements over CDM's project-by-project approach
India's CDM legacy: second largest CDM host after China — strategic implication for transition to Article 6.4 and ongoing revenue streams

concepts.name: Overall Mitigation in Global Emissions (OMGE): Mandatory Cancellation
key_dimensions: OMGE requires that a share of A6.4ERs be cancelled (not transferred) to deliver net global emission reductions — not just a zero-sum transfer
OMGE applies ONLY to Article 6.4, NOT to Article 6.2 ITMOs — a critical distinction UPSC could exploit
The mandatory cancellation rate and how it is set by the Supervisory Body — governance angle
Tension between OMGE (environmental integrity) and host country interests (maximising revenue from credits) — a policy trade-off question

concepts.name: Share of Proceeds (SOP): Adaptation Finance Levy
key_dimensions: SOP is a levy on Article 6.4 transactions channelled to the Adaptation Fund — explicit Paris Agreement provision
SOP applies to Article 6.4 ONLY; Article 6.2 has a voluntary/encouraged SOP-equivalent but it is NOT mandatory — another 'only' trap
Rate: 5% of A6.4ERs issued are cancelled for the Adaptation Fund — specific number is examinable
Link to Adaptation Fund: originally under Kyoto/CDM, now formally anchored to Paris Agreement through Article 6.4 SOP — institutional continuity

concepts.name: Authorization by Host Country: Sovereign Gate in Carbon Markets
key_dimensions: Under Article 6.2 and 6.4, the host country must 'authorise' the transfer of ITMOs/A6.4ERs — this is a legally significant sovereign act
Authorization can be granted, withheld, or revoked before first transfer — post-transfer revocation is NOT permitted (Paris Agreement rulebook)
Difference between authorising a project for NDC use vs. OMIP use — affects whether CA is triggered and at what time
India's Article 6 authorization framework: Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) 2023 under Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022 — domestic implementation angle

concepts.name: India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) 2023 and Article 6 Interface
key_dimensions: CCTS established under Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022 — Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) as nodal body, not a new agency
Two types of carbon credits under CCTS: compliance market credits (for obligated entities) vs. offset credits (voluntary) — domestic architecture mirrors Article 6 duality
How CCTS-generated credits could be authorised as ITMOs for export under Article 6.2 — the sovereign gate and revenue potential for India
Risk of 'hot air' credits: if domestic baseline is weak, exported ITMOs could undermine global climate ambition — a current affairs controversy

concepts.name: Voluntary Carbon Markets (VCMs) vs. Article 6 Compliance Markets
key_dimensions: VCMs (Verra VCS, Gold Standard) operate outside UNFCCC — credits are not ITMOs and do not require corresponding adjustments unless authorised by host country
CORSIA (ICAO's aviation offsetting scheme) can use both VCM credits AND Article 6.2 ITMOs — the interface and eligibility criteria are examinable
The 'Paris Agreement alignment' problem: VCM credits sold to companies for net-zero claims may undermine host country NDCs if no CA is made — the double-counting risk at corporate level
Trend toward 'Article 6-authorised' VCM credits: market premium for credits with CA vs. without — a new market dynamic post-Glasgow

concepts.name: CORSIA (Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation) and Article 6
key_dimensions: CORSIA is under ICAO, not UNFCCC — but it is the largest single buyer of carbon credits globally, making it central to Article 6 market demand
CORSIA Eligible Units (CEUs): can include A6.4ERs and authorised ITMOs from Article 6.2 — linkage between two separate international frameworks
Baseline year controversy: COVID-19 distorted 2019–2020 baseline, affecting the volume of offsets airlines must purchase — a current affairs angle
India's position: Indian carriers (Air India, IndiGo) subject to CORSIA from 2027 Phase 2 — domestic compliance cost and Article 6 supply opportunity simultaneously

concepts.name: Additionality and Baseline Setting in Article 6.4: Environmental Integrity
key_dimensions: Additionality: a project must show emissions reductions would NOT have occurred without carbon finance — the core integrity test, and historically the most gamed aspect of CDM
Baseline approaches under 6.4 Supervisory Body: project-specific, standardised, and conservative baselines — shift away from CDM's project-by-project manipulation
Permanence risk (especially for forestry/land-use credits): how Article 6.4 addresses reversal through buffer pools and insurance mechanisms
Methodological transition: COP28 Dubai controversy over Supervisory Body's draft methodologies being rejected by CMA — governance tension between technical body and political body

concepts.name: Transition of CDM Credits (CERs) to Article 6.4: Grandfathering Rules
key_dimensions: Decision at COP26: CDM projects registered after 2013 with crediting periods extending to 2020 can apply for transition — specific eligibility window is examinable
CERs issued before 2013 are NOT eligible for transition — this cut-off is a classic UPSC 'exception' trap

Transition vs. carry-over distinction: CDM projects transition to Article 6.4 methodology; old CERs for Kyoto compliance cannot be used for Paris NDCs (no carry-over for Annex I countries' Kyoto surplus)
India angle: thousands of Indian CDM projects — economic value at stake and the lobbying India did for a more liberal transition rule

concepts.name: Article 6.4 Supervisory Body: Composition, Powers, and Accountability
key_dimensions: Composition: 12 members (2 per UN regional group + 1 SIDS + 1 LDC) — specific formula unlike most UNFCCC bodies
Reports to CMA, not to UNFCCC Secretariat or SBSTA directly — a governance chain that matters for understanding accountability
Powers: approve methodologies, accredit DOEs, register projects, issue A6.4ERs — compare to CDM Executive Board which had similar powers under Kyoto
COP28 drama: CMA rejected the Supervisory Body's draft rules on methodologies and removals — rare instance of political override of technical body, signalling governance fragility

concepts.name: Carbon Removals and Sinks under Article 6.4: The Contentious New Frontier
key_dimensions: Article 6.4 explicitly includes 'removals' (carbon dioxide removal — CDR) unlike CDM which was largely mitigation/avoidance focused
Types: nature-based (REDD+, blue carbon, soil carbon) vs. technology-based (DACCS, BECCS) — different permanence and verification challenges
Accounting problem: removal credits are inherently reversible (a forest can burn) — how the rulebook addresses this without creating a 'hot air' market
COP28 controversy: draft rules on removals were among the sections rejected by CMA — unresolved status means a live current affairs issue for UPSC 2025–26

concepts.name: REDD+ and Its Relationship with Article 6: Overlapping Frameworks
key_dimensions: REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation) was established under UNFCCC pre-Paris — it is NOT the same as Article 6, but can feed into it
REDD+ results can be transferred as ITMOs under Article 6.2 if the host country authorises and applies corresponding adjustments — the linkage mechanism
Risk of double claiming: country counts REDD+ results toward its NDC AND sells them as ITMOs — requires strict accounting under Article 6 rulebook
India's forest cover and REDD+ potential: India's NDC includes carbon sink targets — selling forest-based ITMOs would reduce this NDC headroom, a strategic tension

concepts.name: Non-Market Approaches under Article 6.8: Scope and Significance
key_dimensions: Article 6.8 covers: mitigation, adaptation, finance, technology transfer, capacity building — deliberately broad to include actions that cannot be monetised
Glasgow Committee on Non-Market Approaches (CNMA) established to operationalise 6.8 — a specific institutional body to know
No corresponding adjustments, no credit issuance, no trading — purely cooperative/facilitative in nature; key distinction from 6.2 and 6.4
Why 6.8 matters for developing countries: not all climate action is amenable to carbon markets; 6.8 protects space for public-good climate cooperation — a North-South equity argument

concepts.name: Paris Agreement's 'Ratchet Mechanism' and Carbon Market Integrity
key_dimensions: NDCs must represent 'progression' over time (Article 4.3) — selling cheap early-vintage ITMOs risks locking in low ambition baselines for future NDC cycles
The 'hot air' problem: if a country's NDC target is weak, it can sell surplus ITMOs without real-world emission reductions — undermines the ratchet
Relationship between Article 6 and Global Stocktake (Article 14): GST assesses collective progress, which should feed back into NDC ambition and thus carbon market supply quality
India's evolving NDC (2022 update): 45% emissions intensity reduction by 2030 — how this target interacts with Article 6 sales strategy is a live policy question

concepts.name: Just Transition and Sustainable Development Co-Benefits Requirements in Article 6.4
key_dimensions: Article 6.4 explicitly requires projects to contribute to sustainable development — host country defines SD criteria (unlike CDM where host country had discretion but no structured requirement)
Stakeholder consultation and environmental/social safeguards: mandatory under 6.4 Supervisory Body rules — stronger than CDM's voluntary Gold Standard add-on
Gender-responsive approaches: Paris Agreement and Article 6 rulebook include gender considerations — an often-missed dimension in UPSC prep
Tension between SD co-benefits and cost-competitiveness: projects with strong co-benefits may be costlier, reducing their attractiveness to buyers seeking cheap credits

concepts.name: Geopolitical Dimensions: India, China, and the Article 6 Negotiating Blocs
key_dimensions: BASIC group (Brazil, South Africa, India, China) historically pushed for broad CDM transition and flexible Article 6.2 rules — negotiating continuity

Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDC) vs. High Ambition Coalition (HAC): Article 6 integrity rules were a fault line — LMDC wanted looser rules to maximise credit supply, HAC wanted strict corresponding adjustments
Brazil's long resistance to corresponding adjustments (wanted to count NDC achievement AND sell ITMOs) — finally resolved at COP26; Brazil's position shift is examinable
Article 6 as a climate finance mechanism for India: potential annual market of billions of dollars — RBI and SEBI roles in regulating cross-border carbon credit flows under FEMA framework
